whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam for?

personas.label: DevOps Engineers
personas.description: You run Salesforce deployments today and want to show you can design the whole pipeline, from sandbox to production.

personas.label: Release Managers
personas.description: You plan releases across several teams and need to choose the right environments, tools and test steps.

personas.label: Platform Architects
personas.description: This is one of the four exams you need for System Architect, alongside Platform Developer I, Integration Architect and Identity and Access Management Architect.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a practical exam. You need to know the sandbox types and their refresh limits, what each deployment tool can and can't do, and how to recover when a production deployment goes wrong.
bullets: 65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers. Many questions turn on small differences between change sets, the Salesforce CLI and unlocked packages.
Real-world problems. Expect questions on deleting metadata, deployment order and what to do when there is no built-in rollback.
Pipeline design. You need to know how source control, scratch orgs and automated tests fit together in CI/CD.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have run releases for a team do best. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and make sure you can draw an environment plan for a project with several teams.

examFormat.heading: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions are short scenarios about a team, a project or a failed release. You choose the right sandbox, tool or order of steps.
bestWayToPass: Learn the sandbox table: Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy and Full. Know how much data each holds and how often it can be refreshed.
Know the limits of change sets: They can't delete metadata, only work between connected orgs, and leave no history in source control.
Understand source-driven development: Version control is the source of truth, and orgs are built from it.
Know the test rules: Production deployments with Apex need 75% overall code coverage, and you choose which tests run.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you plan environments, manage releases and move changes safely from development to production using sandboxes, source control, packages and the Salesforce CLI.

keyConcepts.h2: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Org Strategy: Sandboxes and Scratch Orgs
blocks.body: Each sandbox type has a job. **Developer** sandboxes copy metadata only, hold 200 MB of data and can be refreshed every day. They suit one developer. **Developer Pro** is the same with 1 GB of data, which helps for bigger test data sets. **Partial Copy** includes metadata plus a sample of data chosen by a sandbox template, holds 5 GB and can be refreshed every 5 days. It suits QA and training. **Full** copies all data and metadata and can be refreshed every 29 days. It is the only safe place for performance testing and final user testing. **Scratch orgs** are short-lived orgs built from source and a definition file. They last up to 30 days and are used for package development and automated tests.

blocks.heading: Version Control and Source-Driven Development
blocks.body: In source-driven development, the code in Git is the truth, not any one org. Developers pull from Git, work in a sandbox or scratch org, and push their changes back with the Salesforce CLI. A common branching model has a main branch that matches production, a branch per release or environment, and a short-lived branch per feature. Merges go through pull requests, so someone reviews every change. This gives you a history of who changed what and a way to rebuild any environment. It also fixes the biggest problem with change sets: nothing is lost when a sandbox is refreshed.

blocks.heading: CI/CD Pipelines: Salesforce CLI and Packages
blocks.body: A pipeline runs the same steps every time code is merged: check out the code, deploy to a test org, run Apex tests, and report the result. The **Salesforce CLI** does the deploying. You can **validate** a deployment against production ahead of time and then **quick deploy** it later without running the tests again, as long as it is within 10 days. **Unlocked packages** group related metadata into a versioned unit you can install and upgrade, which makes large orgs easier to split up. **DevOps Center** gives admins a point-and-click way to work with Git-based pipelines. **Change sets** are still fine for small teams but don't scale.

blocks.heading: Testing in the Deployment Pipeline
blocks.body: Apex code needs at least 75% overall test coverage to deploy to production, and every trigger needs some coverage. You choose the test level: **RunLocalTests** (the default for production when Apex is in the deployment), **RunSpecifiedTests** (faster, but each class in the deployment then needs 75% coverage from the tests you pick), or **RunAllTestsInOrg**. Beyond unit tests, plan for integration testing in a Partial Copy sandbox, user acceptance testing in a Full sandbox, and regression testing before each release. Tests should create their own data and not depend on data in the org.

blocks.heading: Release Management and Deployment Order
blocks.body: Some things must be deployed in order: objects and fields before the layouts and code that use them, and permission sets after the fields they grant. Some changes can't be deployed with metadata at all, such as certain org settings, and need a written manual step. **Destructive changes** (deleting metadata) need a destructiveChanges.xml file and can't be done with change sets. Salesforce has no one-click rollback, so the plan is to keep the last good version in Git and redeploy it, and to use feature flags such as custom metadata to switch new features off. Schedule big releases around the three Salesforce seasonal releases and test in a preview sandbox first.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions ask for the right environment, tool or order of steps for a given team. Look for clues about team size, how much data is needed and how often changes ship.

blocks.heading: Sandbox Strategy
blocks.body: Developers get Developer sandboxes. QA uses Partial Copy. Performance and final user testing use Full. If a question mentions realistic data volumes, the answer is a Full sandbox.

blocks.heading: Change Set Limitations
blocks.body: Change sets can't delete metadata, can't move between unrelated orgs and don't keep history. When a scenario needs any of those, look for the CLI or packages.

blocks.heading: Source-Driven Development
blocks.body: If the team keeps losing work when sandboxes are refreshed, or can't tell who changed what, the answer is version control with source-driven development.

blocks.heading: Package Development (2GP)
blocks.body: Unlocked packages split a large org into versioned modules. Managed packages are for ISVs selling on AppExchange. Both are built with scratch orgs and a Dev Hub.

blocks.heading: CI/CD Pipeline Design
blocks.body: Every merge should trigger a deploy and test run. Validate against production early, then quick deploy in the release window.

nextCertsAfter.intro: After this exam, most people complete the other System Architect exams and then aim for CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: A team needs to run performance tests with the same data volume as production before a big release. Which environment should they use?
options: Full sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Scratch org
Developer sandbox
sampleQuestions.explanation: Only a Full sandbox has a complete copy of production data, so it is the only place where performance results mean something.
whyWrong: A Partial Copy sandbox has only a sample of data, so load times won't match production.
Scratch orgs start empty and are meant for development, not load testing.
A Developer sandbox has no production data and only 200 MB of storage.

sampleQuestions.question: An admin needs to delete three unused custom fields from production as part of a release. The team uses change sets today. What should they do?
options: Refresh production from a sandbox
Use a destructiveChanges.xml file with the Salesforce CLI
Add the fields to an outbound change set marked for deletion
Remove the fields from all page layouts
sampleQuestions.explanation: Change sets can't delete metadata. A destructive changes manifest deployed with the CLI or Metadata API can.
whyWrong: You can't refresh production from a sandbox.
There is no deletion option in change sets.
Removing fields from layouts hides them but doesn't delete them.

sampleQuestions.question: A deployment was validated against production on Monday and passed all tests. The release window is Thursday. How can they deploy quickly on Thursday?
options: Run the whole validation again on the Thursday
Deploy with a change set instead
Deploy with RunAllTestsInOrg
Quick deploy the validated deployment
sampleQuestions.explanation: A validated deployment can be quick deployed within 10 days without running the tests again, which keeps the release window short.
whyWrong: Running validation again repeats the slow test run you already did.
A new change set would need its own tests in production.
Running all tests would be even slower.

sampleQuestions.question: Developers keep losing their work when the shared Developer Pro sandbox is refreshed. They also can't tell who changed what. What is the best fix?
options: Use a Full sandbox instead
Adopt version control and source-driven development
Ask each of the developers to keep notes in a shared spreadsheet
Refresh the sandbox less often
sampleQuestions.explanation: With Git as the source of truth, a sandbox refresh loses nothing, and every change has a history with an author.
whyWrong: A Full sandbox can be refreshed too, and still has no change history.
A spreadsheet is manual, unreliable and not a real record of changes.
Refreshing less often only delays the problem.

sampleQuestions.question: A deployment uses RunSpecifiedTests. What coverage rule applies?
options: Only triggers need coverage
The whole org must have 90% coverage
Each class and trigger needs 75% coverage
No coverage is needed when tests are specified
sampleQuestions.explanation: With RunSpecifiedTests, every class and trigger in the package must reach 75% coverage from the tests you chose.
whyWrong: Classes need coverage too, not only triggers.
90% is not a Salesforce requirement.
Coverage rules still apply. They just apply per class instead of org-wide.

sampleQuestions.question: A large org has five teams changing the same metadata. Releases often break each other's work. What should the architect recommend to split the org into independent parts?
options: Managed packages published on the AppExchange
One Full sandbox shared by all teams
Unlocked packages for each team's area
More change sets
sampleQuestions.explanation: Unlocked packages let each team own a versioned set of metadata with clear dependencies, so they can release on their own schedule.
whyWrong: Managed packages are for selling apps to other companies, not for internal teams.
Sharing one sandbox increases collisions instead of reducing them.
More change sets make the problem worse, since nobody can see what overlaps.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about scratch orgs is correct?
options: They are copies of production data
Built from source and a definition file
They remove the need for a Dev Hub entirely
They can be refreshed every 29 days
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scratch orgs are empty orgs created from a definition file. You push source to them and throw them away after use, within 30 days at most.
whyWrong: Scratch orgs start with no production data.
You need a Dev Hub to create scratch orgs.
29 days is the refresh interval for Full sandboxes.

sampleQuestions.question: A release went live and broke a key process. Salesforce has no rollback button. What is the best plan for next time?
options: Keep the old version in source control, use feature flags
Skip running any of the tests so the deployment is faster
Always deploy on Fridays
Never deploy Apex
sampleQuestions.explanation: With the last good version in Git you can redeploy it quickly. Feature flags, such as a custom metadata setting, let you turn a feature off without a deployment.
whyWrong: Skipping tests increases the chance of breaking production.
Deploying on a certain day doesn't make rollback possible.
Avoiding Apex isn't realistic and doesn't address rollback.

sampleQuestions.question: The QA team needs a test environment with realistic sample data from several objects, refreshed about once a week. Which sandbox fits best?
options: Scratch org
Developer sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Partial Copy sandbox copies a sample of production data using a template and can be refreshed every 5 days.
whyWrong: Scratch orgs start empty and need data loaded by script.
Developer sandboxes have no production data.
Developer Pro also copies metadata only, with no production data.

sampleQuestions.question: A deployment fails because a page layout refers to a field that doesn't exist in production yet. What is the right fix?
options: Include the field, or deploy it first
Delete the layout
Run all tests
Deploy the layout first, then the field
sampleQuestions.explanation: Metadata that is referenced must exist before or alongside the metadata that uses it. Deploy the field with the layout or before it.
whyWrong: Deleting the layout loses work and isn't needed.
Tests don't fix a missing dependency.
Deploying the layout first is what caused the failure.

sampleQuestions.question: An admin team with little Git experience wants to move away from change sets and start using source control, using clicks rather than the command line. What should they look at?
options: Workbench
Data Loader
Ant Migration Tool
DevOps Center
sampleQuestions.explanation: DevOps Center gives a point-and-click interface on top of Git and pipelines, designed for admins and low-code teams.
whyWrong: Workbench is a utility for queries and simple deploys, not a pipeline tool.
Data Loader moves data, not metadata.
The Ant Migration Tool is command-line and is being retired.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the minimum overall Apex code coverage needed to deploy to production?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Salesforce requires at least 75% overall coverage, and every trigger must have some coverage.
whyWrong: 50% is below the requirement.
65% is below the requirement.
100% is a good goal but not the rule.

sampleQuestions.question: Salesforce's next seasonal release is in six weeks. The team wants to test their custom code against it before production is upgraded. What should they do?
options: Create a new Developer Edition org
Refresh a sandbox onto preview before the cutoff
Ask Salesforce to delay the upgrade
Wait until production has been upgraded and then test it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sandboxes on a preview instance get the new release a few weeks before production. Refreshing in time puts a sandbox on preview so you can test early.
whyWrong: A Developer Edition org doesn't have your org's code or setup.
Salesforce doesn't delay releases for single customers.
Testing after the upgrade means any problems hit users first.

sampleQuestions.question: A team wants every pull request to be tested automatically before it is merged. What is the core of the pipeline?
options: Emailing changes to the release manager
A change set uploaded manually for every pull request
A CI job that deploys to a test org and runs tests
A weekly manual deployment
sampleQuestions.explanation: Continuous integration runs the same deploy and test steps on every change, so problems are found before the merge.
whyWrong: Email isn't a pipeline and adds no testing.
Change sets can't be automated from a pull request.
A weekly manual deploy finds problems late.

sampleQuestions.question: Tests pass in the sandbox but fail in production because they rely on records that exist only in the sandbox. What should be changed?
options: Use SeeAllData=true in all tests
Lower the coverage target
Copy all of the sandbox data into production
Make the tests create their own test data
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tests should build the data they need, using test setup methods or factories. Then they behave the same in every org.
whyWrong: SeeAllData makes tests depend on org data, which is the cause of the problem.
Lowering coverage doesn't fix failing tests, and 75% is fixed.
Copying test records into production pollutes real data.
